#8012. Breaking: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (231 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Stop Early, Stay Simple: Evidence Acquisition for Power System Fault and Attack Diagnosis

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (231 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.21695v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Diagnostic models for cyber-physical power systems usually inspect every telemetry source for every event, although some events are clear from one source and others need several. We ask when a learned policy for choosing that evidence is worth its added complexity. To answer this, we present ActiGrid, a benchmark framework for active evidence acquisition that pairs a classifier trained to tolerate missing modalities with a Double Deep Q-Network (DQN), which either requests another source or stops and diagnoses but never operates grid actuators. On the public TU Delft digital substation and MSU/ORNL power system attack benchmarks, we compare the DQN with fixed subsets and orders, calibrated entropy stopping, a greedy value of information rule, and tree ensembles trained per subset. The learned policy does adapt to what it observes, yet it is statistically indistinguishable from entropy stopping on TU Delft and Pareto dominated by simple controls on MSU/ORNL, while compact subset classifiers outperform it while reading fewer sources on both benchmarks. Entropy stopping run over those subset classifiers reaches the highest mean Macro-F1 on TU Delft (0.928 while reading 57% of the sources) but brings no saving over a static three source subset on MSU/ORNL, where no method exceeds 0.45 Macro-F1. Selective acquisition can pay off, but on these benchmarks it does not need a learned policy.

#8009. TIBECG: Temporal Information Bottleneck for Lead-Specific Demographic Privacy in ECG Waveform Release

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (194 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

TIBECG: Temporal Information Bottleneck for Lead-Specific Demographic Privacy in ECG Waveform Release

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21694v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transmitting an electrocardiogram (ECG) waveform can expose demographic information beyond an intended diagnostic task. We evaluate TIBECG, an architectural temporal information bottleneck, on individual leads extracted from hospital twelve-lead recordings. A 2,302,337-parameter processor varies its latent length while retaining the same nine-score consistency objective, without age or sex labels in protector fitting. Across 6,386 recordings, ten folds, 12 leads and 21 lengths, retrospective selections retained at least 95% of each lead's clean macro-F1. Their weaker age/sex interval gain exceeded the best eligible conventional transformation on all leads, by a median 22.08 percentage points. The implemented sampling-rate comparison shows that direct downsampling usually suppresses demographic inference more strongly but at a larger loss of diagnostic utility, whereas TIBECG favors utility preservation. Selection stability also varies by lead. Lower latent Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence does not reliably rank residual sex leakage at a fixed length. These findings support lead-specific evaluation of waveform processing, not validated consumer deployment or expert-readable reconstruction. When the waveform-input diagnostic classifier is hosted as part of a proprietary cloud service rather than deployed on the device, waveform transmission is required to obtain its scores.

#8006. Tech Report: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (238 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: AdaFlowLite: Scalable and Non-blocking Inference on Asynchronous Mobile Data

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (238 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rise of mobile devices equipped with numerous sensors, such as LiDAR and cameras, has driven the adoption of multi-modal deep intelligence for distributed sensing tasks, such as smart cabins and driving assistance. However, the arrival time of mobile sensory data vary due to modality size and network dynamics, which can lead to delays (if waiting for slow data) or accuracy decline (if inference proceeds without waiting). Moreover, the diversity and dynamic nature of mobile systems exacerbate this challenge. In response, we present a shift to \textit{opportunistic} inference for asynchronous distributed multi-modal data, enabling inference as soon as partial data arrives. While existing methods focus on optimizing modality consistency and complementarity, known as modal affinity, they lack a \textit{computational} approach to control this affinity in open-world mobile environments. % \sysname pioneers the formulation of structured cross-modality affinity in mobile contexts using a hierarchical analysis-based normalized matrix. This approach accommodates the diversity and dynamics of modalities, generalizing across different types and numbers of inputs. Employing an multi-modal lightweight Swin Transformer (MMLST), \sysname facilitates real-time and flexible data imputation, adapting to various modalities and downstream tasks without retraining. Experiments show that \sysname significantly reduces inference latency by up to 80.4\% and enhances accuracy by up to 62.1\%, while achieving nearly a 50\% reduction in energy consumption, outperforming status quo approaches. Also, this method can enhance LLM performance to preprocess asynchronous data.

#8002. EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (218 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

EgoLink: Egocentric Language-Vision Interactive Network Knowledge Challenge Summary

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (218 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.

#8000. FCP: Formal Context Protocol for Verifying LLM-Generated Artifacts

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (204 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

FCP: Formal Context Protocol for Verifying LLM-Generated Artifacts

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (204 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21679v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: When a language model writes both an artifact and the tests meant to check it, a passing test is weak evidence: one misreading of the request yields a faulty artifact and a check that accepts it. We present the Formal Context Protocol (FCP), which checks AI-generated artifacts against the request itself. FCP separates conformance (does the artifact satisfy a formal reading of a requirement?), which model checkers and SMT solvers decide, from fidelity (does the reading mean what the prose means?), which has no decision procedure but is refutable by a concrete witness. Eight ways a proof can falsely certify a requirement each become a mechanical check that returns a witness, and what no machine can settle becomes concrete questions for the request's author. Adapters place hardware, text, agents and code on the same engines. On four hardware designs, trusting AI-written assertions certified 23% of violated requirements, and FCP certified none. On ten code tasks, code from three language models passed its own tests and violated the request every time. Trusting the tests certified all 33 violations, and FCP certified three. Agreement among models, readings or tests did not imply correctness.

#7996. Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (257 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.21669v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

#7995. Industry News: Simplifying multicloud networking to Azure with partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (590 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Simplifying multicloud networking to Azure with partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (590 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as AI changes how businesses build and run applications, more enterprises are spreading their models, data and applications across multiple clouds.
  • We wanted to make that much simpler.
  • According to recent reports, "Google Cloud partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect simplifies multi-cloud networking with a direct cloud-native approach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Director, Product Management, Cloud Networking.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Sources indicate that as AI changes how businesses build and run applications, more enterprises are spreading their models, data and applications across multiple clouds. To make that work, they need fast, private connections between those environments. Historically, connecting multiple clouds has meant ordering physical connections from each provider, setting up networking on both sides, and coordinating across multiple teams. That process could take weeks or even months.

We wanted to make that much simpler. Today, we're extending partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect to Microsoft Azure, now available in preview. The service is jointly supported by Google Cloud and Microsoft, and gives you a private, high-bandwidth connection between your Google Cloud and Azure environments that’s set up programmatically in minutes, with no physical infrastructure to manage.

According to recent reports, "Google Cloud partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect simplifies multi-cloud networking with a direct cloud-native approach. By removing traditional infrastructure complexity, it provides a reliable, scalable foundation for connecting workloads across different cloud environments." - Ralf Huebenthal, Global Head of IT & Digital Platforms, Nestlé.

“Walmart runs a seamless platform across multiple cloud providers to accelerate innovations. We partner with Google Cloud to leverage their global network for hybrid and multicloud networking. With Cross-Cloud Interconnect, we were able to simplify connectivity between cloud providers, shorten time to production, and reduce overall costs.” - Gerald Bothello, Group Director of Software Engineering, Walmart.

Industry observers note that on-demand connectivity in minutes, not weeks. Set up your connection from the Google Cloud console or API, pick the bandwidth you need, and both clouds handle the rest — no hardware to order, no manual network configuration, and no back and forth between providers.

Built-in reliability. Your connection runs across physically separate locations for redundancy. Google Cloud and Azure jointly monitor the connection and handle maintenance and recovery for you.

In a recent development, private and secure. Your traffic stays off the public internet, and is automatically encrypted between the Google Cloud and Azure edge routers, with no customer configuration required.

Industry observers note that predictable pricing. You pay a fixed price for the connection's bandwidth, so your Google Cloud costs are easy to plan and manage.

Sources indicate that "Customers are building applications, data platforms and AI across more than one cloud, and they want the network between those clouds to just work. Azure Multicloud Interconnect with Google Cloud gives customers a private, managed path between Azure and Google Cloud, and we're excited to work with Google Cloud to bring it to customers in public preview." - Sudha Mahajan, Partner, Product Management, Azure Networking, Microsoft.

Our Cross-Cloud Interconnect ecosystem continues to expand:.

In a recent development, partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect for Microsoft Azure is available in preview today in us-east4 (N. Virginia), us-west2 (Los Angeles), and europe-west3 (Frankfurt), alongside the generally available AWS and OCI offerings. We'll add more regions as the Azure offering moves to general availability.

Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect for last mile with Lumen is available in preview, for customers connecting their private clouds, on-premises sites, and neocloud environments to Google Cloud.

It has been revealed that partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect is built on an open specification for network interoperability. Google Cloud collaborated with AWS and published it last year, and any provider can adopt it.

To learn more, visit the partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect documentation, read Microsoft's announcement, or contact your Google Cloud account team.

#7991. Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (249 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Depth-Aware Activation Steering via Attention Residuals

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (249 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21655v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Activation steering is a simple, training-free way to modulate LLM behavior, yet existing methods typically inject vectors at a single layer and lack mechanisms for depth-aware propagation or internal verification. We combine two recent ideas - Attention Residuals (AttnRes) providing learnable cross-layer pathways, and Jacobian-lens (J-space) concept readout - into a lightweight depth-aware steering pipeline. On two small open models (Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-0.8B), distributing a persona vector according to AttnRes-style depth weights yields stronger internal alignment (deeper-layer concept cosine and rank, p<0.0001) and stronger behavioral shifts than single-layer injection. The effect is sign-specific: reverse vectors invert all six metrics, random directions degrade alignment (p<0.0001), and a short LoRA fine-tune erases the imprint. Injection rewires attention strictly downstream of the injection point (upstream JS = 0.00000). Three practical findings follow. First, a layer-wise geometric decomposition of cosine readouts: at the injection layer 123% of the increase is arithmetic, while 5-11 layers downstream 100% is dynamical. Second, an intensity window: effects are monotone over 0.3-0.7, then generation collapses (617 to 306 to 25 chars). Third, metric discipline: keyword-rule metrics fail LLM-judge validation (kappa <= 0.09), and two rule-based conclusions were retracted. Training the depth weights on a steering objective (200 steps, frozen backbone) raises final alignment 10x on held-out prompts. Cross-persona vectors retain 96-99% of the effect: specificity holds against random, not semantic, directions. We contribute a practical, low-overhead depth-aware steering method with a careful evaluation protocol. Code and data are released.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Evaluating Semantic Insensitivity in Financial Sentiment Analysis: Implications for Sustainable Financial Decision-Making

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (180 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21653v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Financial sentiment analysis is critical for automated trading, portfolio management, and risk assessment, heavily relying on models like FinBERT. Despite high benchmark accuracy, these models remain vulnerable to subtle adversarial text modifications, threatening the integrity of algorithmic decision-making. In this paper, we propose Agent-driven Semantic Inversion (ASI), a novel adversarial attack framework targeting financial sentiment models through domain-specific semantic manipulation. Utilizing an LLM-powered multi-agent pipeline, our approach identifies eligible financial news sentences and applies targeted lexical substitutions. We empirically evaluate ASI against FinBERT, one of the most widely deployed financial sentiment models. Our results reveal a striking vulnerability: the attack successfully deceived FinBERT in 90.85% of eligible cases, with the model frequently maintaining its original sentiment prediction despite the fundamental inversion of financial performance indicators. Through qualitative analysis and token-level investigation, we demonstrate that FinBERT critically over-relies on contextual keywords and syntactic patterns rather than true logical comprehension of financial semantics. Our findings highlight the urgent need for logic-aware, robust financial NLP models to ensure the reliability of automated decision-making systems.

#7987. How to Build Durable Agentic Systems with Google Antigravity: From Instructions to Loops

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2505 w)

How to Build Durable Agentic Systems with Google Antigravity: From Instructions to Loops

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I watched the discussion on agentic loops grow louder over the past few months.
  • You can categorize the work that we give to our agents into five distinct tiers, scaling from a quick question up through Agile tasks, stories, and epics to a continuous system:.
  • A simple question: This does not require an agent; an assistant can answer it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developer Relations, Antigravity.

Industry observers note that I watched the discussion on agentic loops grow louder over the past few months. But for me, the reality is simpler: prompt engineering has shifted from individual tasks to systems design, and the harness around the model (not the model itself) is now my primary constraint in software engineering. In this article, I'll show you how to build and verify those harnesses so you can move from single-turn instructions to durable agentic loops in Google Antigravity.

You can categorize the work that we give to our agents into five distinct tiers, scaling from a quick question up through Agile tasks, stories, and epics to a continuous system:.

A simple question: This does not require an agent; an assistant can answer it.

Industry observers note that A task / idea: This is one where a single prompt can zero-shot it. Use Google AI Studio to promptly transform ideas to functional prototypes.

According to recent reports, an app / larger feature / story: The kind of work that required weekly planning and splitting into subtasks before AI. Use loops for execution and full-featured agents, like Google Antigravity. This tier is also where your steering moves upstream: You lock in the spec, the plan, and the executable tests before any loop runs.

A project / epic: A few features that make a cohesive story when connected. Loops here might help with planning too. This is also where one needs to go beyond simple turn-based prompting.

A system: An overview of all of the projects and tasks. This is where you write AGENTS.md project instructions, create skills, set up sidecars, wire up verification gates, and configure an instrument cluster to keep themselves on top of everything. Loops at this level make the biggest difference and come with similarly higher risks.

Figure 1: Five tiers of engineering work, from single prompts to verified agentic loops.

The baseline of software development is shifting. This shift represents a basic law of human nature: we seek the highest leverage possible, moving from manual labor to delegation, and finally to orchestration. Because attention is the fresh bottleneck, anything that lets the work continue with less interruption could make a move in the right direction. By early 2026, empirical research of open-source projects estimated that coding agent adoption had reached between 22% and 29% of more than 128,000 active repositories on GitHub. Those who become proficient in agentic workflows now operate with a level of leverage that elevates their entire team's productivity. However, it also increases the cognitive load on everyone who is taking responsibility at the systemic level.

To understand this shift, let's trace the technical lineage of loops and set some high level expectations.

The academic seed was Yao et al.'s ReAct paper in October 2022, which interleaved reasoning traces with tool calls. ReAct beat reinforcement learning baselines by 34% on ALFWorld and 10% on WebShop by reasoning before acting, mirroring human nature: we perform better when verbalizing plans. Then came AutoGPT in early 2023, raising millions in venture funding. While early iterations of ReAct frequently spun in infinite loops, it proved developers wanted hands-off automation, highlighting the need for structural guardrails.

It has been revealed that in mid-2025, developers ran stateless bash loops that piped prompts into command-line agents and reset context files on every tick. Resetting context prevents cognitive bloat and acknowledges that human memory limits also apply to models. Stateless bash loops worked only because the durable state lived outside the model: in Git history, in progress files, and in the test suite. It successfully built self-hosting compilers over months of automated runs. By spring 2026, major tool environments absorbed this pattern, shipping native commands like /goal to let agents run unattended loops.

Consider a theoretical example:.

In a recent development, if you put your agent in a flat sequential chain to complete multiple tasks in a row, the agent's success rate degrades exponentially. When each of its individual steps operates as an independent probability event, a sequence of N steps has a cumulative success rate of pN. For instance, if you run a task requiring 20 consecutive file modifications with a model that has p = 0.95 accuracy, then you face a success rate of only 36%. Without your structural interventions, they will fail almost certainly.

Recent findings suggest that is 0.95 a real number? Treat it as an illustrative per-step reliability, not as a benchmark result. Even a frontier model reaches reliable multi-step outcomes only when it runs inside a verified harness. If your own per-step reliability sits closer to 75%, then the raw chain is already under 6% by step 10. The verification around the model sets the ceiling, which is why the loop matters.

It has been revealed that this is why you need evaluation loops. A verification gate should not force your agent to retry indefinitely (which causes infinite spinning runaways). Instead, it should pinpoint where the error occurred and allow the model exactly one targeted retry to fix it. If your agent has a 95% base accuracy, and your evaluation loop has a 95% chance of spotting and fixing the error on that single retry, the effective step success probability rises to 0.95 + (0.05 x 0.95) = 99.75%.

Sources indicate that that arithmetic assumes the check is independent of the worker, so the gate has to be an outside check. Compilers, test suites, and linters give you that for free, and behavioral evaluations let you assert on discrete tool calls and intermediate actions in seconds instead of waiting on a full end-to-end benchmark. For semantic judgments that a deterministic test cannot make, I pair models from different families so the reviewer does not share the worker's blind spot.

Even if fixing fails, just spotting the error with a 95% accuracy, lets you jump in and manually realign the system while keeping the same 99.75% subagent accuracy and only paying the cost of human-in-the-loop intervention.

The table below highlights the probability of completion across different chain lengths, comparing raw models to this single-retry course-correction topology:.

If each step in a chain adds approximately 1% of context in tokens, you end up with a chain that is not much longer than 50 steps before we require compression. A 95% base accuracy that can be evaluated (and course corrected with 95% accuracy for each dimension that we care about) should keep you at good success rates for such individual running agents. If you establish a scalable way to divide and conquer problems, you can apply similar principles to drive your subagents. As we can see, at 20 steps, a 95% accuracy paired with a single-retry corrective loop yields a 95% end-to-end success rate (assuming the correction itself stays under our 20 steps soft limit) while keeping context size reasonable. Note that there is no explicit requirement for the correction to be AI or human driven, but rather it needs to produce accurate and verifiable results.

Sources indicate that this is where you divide problems into tasks that require a small number of steps each. If a problem is more complex, it remains approachable, but it must be divided into smaller subproblems, and so on. For our example, this means allocating up to 20 steps for each level agent, task, and trajectory and another 20 steps for the next level supervisory agent to consolidate contributions. To prevent drift, establish separate evaluations at all subagent and supervisory levels with a final acceptance criteria.

It has been revealed that lastly, you must evaluate these metrics at least once for each level to verify that they measure the right target before running automation at a higher level. These are general estimations, but help you promptly decide whether you should split a problem, repeat a step, or commit results and move on.

In practice, your numbers will look different, but the scaling laws will be similar.

What started as a source of friction has now become one of my primary driving curiosities: how do we build automation when we still have a lot to learn about the craft itself? I have a few ideas.

Industry observers note that to build a loop that does not run off a cliff, you must establish core guardrails that will keep accuracy high and will allow us to debug and intervene whenever necessary. Specifically, these are the pillars I identified:.

Durable state: Git-backed checkpoints ensure that your agent can resume work after a crash.

It has been revealed that verification gates: Automated test suites and compilers deterministically check that the changes are correct. Write the acceptance criteria and the tests upstream, before implementation starts, and make one rule explicit in your project instructions: an agent cannot pass a gate by deleting or weakening a test. When done properly, gates can have >95% accuracy. However, you should be on the lookout for edge cases you might have forgotten about. Especially if verification, evaluation, or manual validation success rates diverge for any of your features.

Recent findings suggest that evals: Anything that cannot be deterministically verified but is crucial should have an evaluation or benchmark which you can later inspect for accuracy. Try to write them in a way that will keep answers to a simple yes or no and accuracy high, ideally over 95%. If you're getting results that point to confusion or unexpected failures, you probably need to split the criteria into simpler ones.

Halt conditions: Turn limits (as we saw above, 20 seems to be the sweet spot) and token or dollar cost ceilings stop runs before API budgets get out of control.

Sources indicate that standardized skills and instructions: Reusable utilities, documented in the SKILL.md format, preferably bundled with code and source of truth references. Pair them with an AGENTS.md that holds the project invariants every run load. Skills stay on disk until their description matches the task, so they do not eat into the 20-step context window.

In a recent development, these pillars don't name a model version, but rather a model family. Individual model leads last only weeks. The asset that survives each release is the harness and its processes: the AGENTS.md instructions every run loads, the SKILL.md modules loaded only when relevant, the isolated Cloud Run sandbox where the loop runs around the clock, the deterministic checks, and the cross-model review. When a run fails or you have to intervene, patch your harness along with the code: a new test, a line in AGENTS.md, a note in the skill. The next run inherits the lesson even though its context starts from zero.

In a recent development, platforms like Google Antigravity have codified these patterns (/grill-me and /goal) into built-in primitives, shifting the work from custom scripts to platform capabilities for most straightforward use cases. The same harness files travel with the repository whether you run Google Antigravity 2.0, the agy CLI, or Antigravity inside VS Code, JetBrains, or Cursor. I would encourage you to give these a try. Do remember, however, to keep an eye on trajectory lengths and look for model confusion.

I myself frequently rely on the /goal primitives in Google Antigravity 2.0 when coordinating multi-turn tasks that require extensive validation and measurements before completion. To anchor this execution, use the /grill-me command for an interactive interview to lock in design constraints, invariants, and the tests that decide success before running /goal loops.

Constructing the metrics for this technical article and then editing it is just one example of how I use these execution loops.

By pairing /goal with /grill-me, you can establish an effective pair-programming dynamic: alignment on intent, followed by autonomy in execution.

To understand the evolution of loops, compare two distinct architectures for DIY agentic loops:.

Geoffrey Huntley's "Ralph" loop is a prime example of stateless architecture. Here's the simplest working version of an Antigravity CLI loop:.

While simple, the stateless loop is fragile for multi-file coordination because resetting context discards thinking logs.

A good agent skill could fix much of this limitation by instructing the model to output relevant progress reports in wiki-like markdown files and track changes by looking at git logs.

Still, this complexity has led to developer challenges in larger multi-agent environments, for which custom loops seem to hold the promise.

If you want to write a custom loop from scratch, here is a practical Python implementation using the Google Antigravity SDK. Specifically, this loop does the following actions:.

Initializes a supervisor session.

Verifies the output with the real test suite.

Feeds the actual failure output back for exactly one targeted retry.

Enforces strict call and token budgets.

It has been revealed that not every task inside it is equal, so neither is the model. The supervisor and the implementer run on Gemini 4 Carbon because orchestration, architecture, and the complex fixes need frontier reasoning, codebase search goes to Gemini 4 Hydrogen, and verification goes to a deterministic script that costs no tokens at all. The Guide to AI Tokenomics covers the budgeting side of this split. Far from being a production-ready solution, this is an experimental starting point that you can adapt to suit your individual needs:.

Figure 2: Budgeted supervisory verification loop in the Google Antigravity SDK.

The preceding implementation defines the following budgets:.

max_model_calls=20, a soft limit, counted across the supervisor's whole session.

max_total_tokens=200_000 as the cost ceiling.

According to recent reports, the SDK stops the turn and reports a stop_reason when either one trips. max_retries=1 limits each section: the first attempt plus one fix. If the verification still fails after that, the loop returns False and a human takes the seat instead of the model spinning until the budget runs out.

If you prefer not to build and host your own custom SDK loops from scratch, use Antigravity Agent, an autonomous, asynchronous coding agent. Antigravity Agent operates in a secure, isolated Google Cloud sandbox. This way you can create similar agentic loops by using managed agents to orchestrate execution aims under Google managed infrastructure. Alternatively, you can run the preceding loop inside a long-lived Cloud Run sandbox so that the loop keeps working after you close your laptop.

You must establish a clear boundary for each of your validation systems that lets you  stay in control. No matter how perfect your loop, if you, as the responsible human, cannot sign off on your agent's output, there is minimal value in any of the artifacts it is producing. The good news is that building a quality evaluation scorecard or a loop algorithm uses a similar process to producing any other type of software artifact. So, much of the execution will be automated.

Finally, to make a sound judgment, you should observe each loop from the inside. As you see things working out, with this acquired confidence you step one level up. This is the only way to learn where the agent struggles and how to improve the process itself.

#7984. Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (320 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Consistency Is Not Correction: Separating Confidence, Abstention, and Recovery in LLM Agents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (320 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21651v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A controller that resamples an answer, escalates to a larger model, or abstains is usually justified by a confidence signal. Three claims about such a signal do not follow from one another: it ranks answers (discrimination), it supports withholding some of them (selective prediction), and it changes an answer for the better (correction utility). We give an exact decomposition of the third into gated recoveries minus gated harms, which bounds whether a comparison can succeed before it is run: a gate that only replaces a proposal can act only where the base policy was already wrong, so the initial error count caps the discordant pairs any correct gate can produce. When that cap falls below the count a paired test needs, the experiment cannot return a positive result for a working mechanism, nor distinguish one from a gate that never fired. We measure all three targets on two model scales and find the bound binds. In a small-model suite a perturbation-agreement verifier reaches within-policy AUROC 0.990 (95% interval [0.95, 1.00]) while every episode outcome matches single-sample decoding at 4.32 times the call count. In a controlled 840-episode study no verifier replaced the proposal on any of the 60 GSM8K decisions, so that comparison tested nothing; the entire GSM8K gain across six controllers is one task, and it is the task whose identical temperature-zero repeats disagreed, making it the one answer the service does not reproduce. On the diagnostic set the gate could reach four errors while the test needed six, so even a perfect gate had no significant result available. We report two checks that would have caught this before any budget was spent, and show that tie handling in rankings, tied selection cutoffs, and unequal output limits each move a headline number in the same dataset. The binding constraint on this literature is measurement resolution, not the choice of signal.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (180 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21650v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

arXiv:2611.21649v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (323 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (323 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.21648v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to upcoming tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.

RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (208 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21641v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

Here, we evaluate whether augmenting XAI outputs with textual explanations from multimodal LLMs improves perceived understanding and perceived trust. We conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment ($N = 128$) across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, with and without LLM generated explanations. The explanations improved perceived understanding and perceived trust by 0.35 and 0.26 points on five-point scales (both $p < .001$). The gain appeared in all seven scenarios, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. These results suggest that multimodal LLMs can provide a useful interpretive layer for XAI beyond expert audiences.

Fragmented Markers, Mixed Results: A Systematic Review of AI Coding Assistants and Developer Productivity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (250 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.21632v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding assistants are increasingly embedded in software engineering practice, yet the literature still offers no cumulative, easily interpretable picture of their effects on software developer productivity. The central problem is not a lack of studies, but a lack of comparability: prior work operationalizes productivity through heterogeneous markers, settings, and reporting styles, making cross-study conclusions difficult. To address this, we conduct a staged systematic literature review. In the first stage, we synthesize studies that explicitly examine developer productivity. In the second, we extend the scope to productivity-related developer outcomes using SPACE as a theory-informed lens, capturing human-centered evidence that explicit productivity studies often omit. Across both stages, we analyze how productivity is operationalized, which confounding factors are discussed, and how reported effects are distributed. We identify 187 unique productivity and productivity-related markers, while individual studies typically only use five, revealing a broad but highly fragmented evidence base. Explicit productivity research is dominated by time-, output-, and artifact-oriented proxies, whereas the broader SPACE-aligned corpus makes satisfaction, psychological aspects, and well-being substantially more visible. Reported effects are often positive, but this pattern is stronger in perceived and tendency-based findings than in objective or statistically evaluated ones. Overall, the literature suggests that AI coding assistants can support productivity, but current evidence does not yet support simple, context-independent conclusions. The key contribution of this review is therefore a structured basis for making productivity evidence more interpretable, multidimensional, and comparable across studies.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.18330v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Speech applications require decisions about term presence, turn completion, and language within an audio window. We present Marimba, an interface for typed speech decisions built on frozen Qwen3-ASR 0.6B features. Lexical questions use zero-shot scoring of ASR transcripts; non-lexical questions use a question-conditioned head and a separate layer-18 turn-end readout. Language identification uses the ASR model's own language scores. On private conversational test sets, decoder AUROC is 0.80-0.92; on public read speech it is 0.92-0.97. Speech Commands four-way accuracy is 0.93; binary lexical ECE is at most 0.08. Personal-information detection, which passes the greedy transcript to a private, curated PII pipeline, reaches item-level F1 0.904 on synthetic Brazilian Portuguese speech (1.000 on reference transcripts). Layer-12 speaker readouts detect speaker change with AUROC 0.966-0.980 on AMI and VoxConverse, above an ECAPA baseline, and count speakers (0, 1, 2, or 3+) more accurately than pyannote 3.1. The turn-end readout reaches AUROC 0.930 versus Smart Turn v3.2 at 0.982 on Smart Turn's own test set. On a subset of ICSI meetings labeled by next speaker, AUROC is 0.716 versus 0.712; the paired confidence interval includes zero.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (283 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Continual-ARC: Measuring Skill Acquisition over a Working Lifetime

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (283 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.14505v3 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. We propose Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream built from the three ARC-AGI editions, whose tasks need no domain knowledge. The same tasks return after dormant gaps with fresh instances, while new tasks keep arriving. On each instance, the learner may pay for demonstrations, submit answers, or act inside the harness, with retries permitted on incorrect submissions, which are paid for. Each instance is scored based on the share of this feedback budget consumed. Since a learner may keep anything between instances, memory-based and weight-based systems are scored on the same scale. After the stream, the learner is frozen and tested on fresh instances of the tasks it met, which measures memorization, and on unseen tasks, which measures generalization. We run an agent harness with frozen weights, with and without persistence, on Qwen3.5-9B and GLM-5.3 Flash, comparing them with two prompting floors, a program-induction method and Qwen3.5-9B's weights trained to imitate GLM-5.3 Flash. Persistence in the harness generally does not improve memorization unless provided with explicit expert guidance. Most harness-based methods still learn less than a floor that simply caches each task's demonstrations, across all models we tested. Harness-based methods gain little or nothing on unseen tasks, whereas weight-based learning shows substantial gains. This opens the door to future weight-based continual learning that could teach models to drive harnesses in new domains.

Improved Convergence Rates for Stochastic Multi-Gradient Descent which Close the Gap: A Proof by AI

arXiv:2607.18174v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For smooth nonconvex stochastic multi-objective optimization, stochastic multi-gradient descent (SMG) computes an approximate steepest common descent direction of the objectives from stochastic gradients. Under standard assumptions, this note establishes a fresh convergence rate for SMG in terms of the squared Pareto-stationarity (PS) measure. With a constant stepsize and linearly growing mini-batches, the expected squared empirical PS measure at the algorithm's output is $\tilde{O}(T^{-1})$ after $T$ iterations. This improves on the $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/4})$ bound obtained by Chen et al. (JMLR, 2024) for linearly growing batches, without requiring bounded gradients. Here, $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ suppresses logarithmic factors. The key to the rate improvement is to exploit the Lipschitz continuity of the PS measure, defined by the norm of the multi-gradient descent algorithm (MGDA) direction, rather than the $(1/2)$-H\"older continuity of the MGDA direction used by Chen et al. (2024). For variants of MoCo and MoCo+ with exact MGDA updates and constant batch sizes, the analysis gives expected squared empirical PS rates of $O(T^{-1/2})$ and $\tilde{O}(T^{-2/3})$, respectively. These bounds match the corresponding single-objective momentum rates up to logarithmic factors. The proof was accidentally discovered while the author was preparing homework for a graduate course: ChatGPT 5.4 Thinking Extended generated the initial proof strategy for the main SMG result in response to an author-written homework-solution prompt; the author then verified and reorganized the resulting argument. The appendices document the prompt, summarize the student submissions with LLM disclosures, and present additional proofs and results on momentum-based stochastic MGDA.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (256 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.23202v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

Industry News: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (198 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.23192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.

📅 13 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3212 w)

Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

📅 13 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3212 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.
  • Sources indicate that you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub.
  • Industry observers note that the first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6 and LeRobot 0.7.

Sources indicate that you have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every fresh checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

Industry observers note that the first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type revealed in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for: it drives the robot and reads the results, while the recording itself stays one line of your code. This post walks you through the data loop: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

Where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the loop you build here records a LeRobotDataset with one run(record=...) call, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back with LeRobot's own streaming reader, so the dataset Robot() recorded is exactly the one LeRobot trains on. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so101") records a LeRobotDataset with run(record=...); hf sync syncs it into a Storage Bucket; lerobot-train reads it back over the Hub through LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with a port=. The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

When the agent runs an episode, it invokes one tool, and the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the policy producing every action. Stripped down to the code, the whole loop is a handful of lines:.

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

In a recent development, that's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three, plus the bucket and training items under Advanced. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a placeholder wave function, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

You record new episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

It has been revealed that strands Robots records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware: pass record= to run(), and each run adds one episode. Record the episodes, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The wave function is a placeholder that produces joint targets without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:.

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id is the folder name that follows the bucket, cube_pick here. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

Each sync uploads only the files that changed. Write to the bucket through the day, and publish a versioned copy to a dataset repository when you want one: record="hf://my_user/cube_picking", push=True does that at the end of a run. The placeholder episodes are not useful training data. Pass a trained Policy("") to run() instead.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:.

Sources indicate that the dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync takes it to a bucket: hf sync ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/my_user/cube_picking hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Recent findings suggest that now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

It has been revealed that buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise plans billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

In a recent development, how much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a upcoming file when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. Each run(record=...) starts its own shards, and a lerobot-record session grows its open shard until it fills. Either way, a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus, at most, the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the new chunks and skips the ones already stored.

In a recent development, to train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and it opens a bucket with repo_type="bucket":.

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; StreamingLeRobotDataset reads batches straight from the bucket with only metadata on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

Nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index, plus a seek index for the video shards: a full streaming read of the 86 MB lerobot/svla_so101_pickplace dataset left under 1 MB on disk. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes:.

On macOS, run that from a script with an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, because DataLoader workers start by re-importing the script.

According to recent reports, if you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset you collected trains without a line of fresh code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:.

Buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. --policy.push_to_hub=false keeps the checkpoint local; name a --policy.repo_id to publish it instead. Reach for StreamingLeRobotDataset directly when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop.

The checkpoint lerobot-train writes loads straight back through the same entry point used to run any other policy, so the record-train-deploy loop closes in a few lines:.

A 20-step CPU run of ACT over the two-episode dataset above, streamed from a private bucket, wrote a checkpoint that Policy() loaded and ran on the simulated arm. Twenty steps over placeholder episodes check that the loop connects; it does not train a policy that grasps. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, and a useful ACT policy needs real demonstrations and a GPU.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise aims, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions confirmed as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

In a recent development, in this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post. The keyword argument that changes is port=, which selects the physical arm; id= names its LeRobot calibration, cameras= names the image keys the policy was trained on, and operator= approves its moves.

Recent findings suggest that nothing moves on the real arm until operator= approves it. The demonstrations it records with record= are in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

If your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), nothing in this post changes: a LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, and every step reads it wherever it sits. A bucket adds the Hub-native path, the sync and the streaming read, with no storage to provision first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you record into the same bucket, sync only what changed, and stream it to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format.

Recent findings suggest that the full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the placeholder policy, so no GPU and no Docker are needed, and without a bucket set it needs no Hugging Face credentials either.

In a recent development, run the cells top to bottom. To sync to a bucket, set HF_BUCKET=my-org/robot-fave before starting Jupyter (after hf auth login); each run syncs under its own folder, nb12-, and the notebook streams back from it. Without HF_BUCKET it trains from the local folder instead. To train on a GPU, raise --steps and drop --policy.device=cpu in the training cell.

The snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

Prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions. In Strands Robots an agent cannot record, push, or calibrate, and on a real robot operator= answers every move and every policy run's plan before anything moves.

Sources indicate that training data is a trust boundary. Anything that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Industry observers note that bucket credentials and scope. hf sync and StreamingLeRobotDataset use the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you publish and share.

Overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Sync each collection run to its own path, as in hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. For anything you need to be able to return to, push to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

Recent findings suggest that the loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:.

Recent findings suggest that stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, its last cell prints the command that removes its run. Anything you published to a dataset repository is versioned and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording guide documents run(record=...) and reading a dataset back with LeRobot.

Industry observers note that if you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time, so point each training run at the run_id it should learn from.

It has been revealed that if you want a larger policy than ACT, lerobot-train fine-tunes LeRobot's vision-language-action (VLA) policies, such as SmolVLA and pi0, on the dataset you just streamed, and the checkpoint loads as a Policy the same way. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot(), so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Sources indicate that bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so you can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before you record any of your own.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an issue with what worked and what didn't.

What makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. arXiv:2611.23138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enabling large language models (LLMs) to autonomously conduct training and improve target models is an crucial foundation for recursive self-improvement (RSI). As LLMs expand their role from being trained to conducting training, their model-training capability warrants dedicated study and systematic development. To this end, we construct RSI-Prime, a dataset for improving model-training capability, comprising 350 complete experimental trajectories across seven task categories. To help LLMs learn to make high-quality experimental decisions from training practice, we perform fine-grained decision identification and quality annotation, then apply decision-level loss masking to exclude supervision on low-quality behavior. Experiments with GLM-5.3 on PostTrainBench, a benchmark for autonomous post-training, show that training on RSI-Prime yields a 31.95% relative improvement in overall performance over the original GLM-5.3, highlighting a path toward future RSI systems in which models autonomously sustain their own advancement.
